articles.title_orig: What impact will the Shenzhen summit have on the US-China trade war?
articles.title_zh: What impact will the Shenzhen summit have on the US-China trade war?
articles.content_orig:
Despite warm words between US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping at three-way talks with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Shenzhen Thursday, the simmering trade war between Washington and Beijing still looks to be no closer to resolution.
Issued on: 19/11/2026 - 18:34
Sometimes the meeting is the message.
The three-way talks between Chinese President Xi Jinping , US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin in the Chinese tech capital of Shenzhen Thursday lasted all of 90 minutes .
Just what exactly the three men said to one another through their interpreters during that hour-and-a-half will remain a mystery.
Certainly, the joint “Declaration toward Peace” published afterwards by Beijing and Moscow gave little away: unspecified UN reforms, agreement to boost global oil production, a terse warning to the International Criminal Court and similar global bodies not to “abuse their jurisdiction” and a unanimous agreement that nuclear wars left no winners alive to celebrate.
Read more Historic trilateral summit live: Trump, Xi and Putin agree that a nuclear war must never be fought
While some watchers had warned not to expect any major announcements, others had raised fears that the historic meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation forum would be a new Yalta Conference.
The 1945 summit between the leaders of the allied Soviet Union , United States and Britain decided the shape of the global institutions that would rise out of the ashes of World War II and the fate of the eastern European countries following the defeat of Nazi Germany and its fascist allies.
With Russia’s brutal campaign in Ukraine dragging deeper into its fifth year, Ukraine’s President Volodymyr Zelensky warned against a new meeting between the self-identified superpowers that threatened to once again divide the world up into discrete spheres of influence – regardless of the impact on the peoples who found the borders shifting beneath their feet.
While Beijing and Moscow had both brushed aside comparisons with the conference, the carefully orchestrated spectacle of Xi, Trump and Putin as a 21st-century incarnation of Yalta’s “Big Three” did much to drape the three men with the trappings of World War II-style "great powers".
But speaking to FRANCE 24 in the hours ahead of the meeting, Jean-François Di Meglio, steering committee chair of the Asia Centre think tank, said that parallels between Thursday’s talks and the discussions that ushered in the end of World War II didn’t stand up to scrutiny.
“The term ‘multipolarity’ is essential – and that’s why the comparison that’s often been made with Yalta doesn’t work,” he said. “Because there was a form of membership, a system where each participants’ differences were recognised … Whereas here, what matters most is China’s refusal in principle of a single world order under the aegis of common principles.”

Under the banner of multipolarity, China has for years championed a reworking of the international system that would give more weight to voices from the underdeveloped Global South – of which it has set itself up as an unofficial standard bearer.
Di Meglio said that China’s desire to overturn the Western hegemony that has reigned since the latter half of the 20th century should not be mistaken for altruism.
“While this multipolarity – which is being preached with a certain degree of opportunism, as we can see all too clearly in the way this meeting has been organised – is indeed China’s guiding principle, is it a sincere one or not? It is obvious that everything is being done in China’s best interest.”
Despite the warm words that Trump and Xi had for one another, the talks seem to have done little to resolve the simmering tensions between the two powers. Beijing’s threat last year to withhold critical rare earth exports won them a reprieve from Trump’s trade war , but the truce ends in January.
China has so far been one of the few countries to go toe-to-toe with the US after Trump unleashed a slew of tariffs against allies and adversaries alike, leveraging its unquestioned dominance in the rare earth and critical minerals supply chains that form the bedrock of the world’s cutting-edge technologies.
The US on Monday tightened rules around the export of advanced computing chips crucial for the development of frontier AI , an industry where US corporations still seem to hold an advantage over their Chinese rivals. The rules also restrict Chinese access to overseas data centres that would allow companies to access advanced computing power remotely.
With the Democrats having seized the House and Senate from Trump’s Republicans in the midterm elections earlier this month, Di Meglio said that foreign policy would become even more central to the president’s final two years in office.
“Artificial intelligence has raw materials, and those raw materials are rare earths,” he said. “And in Donald Trump’s mind, figuring out how to break this deadlock must be very, very high on his list of priorities.”

While the US has begun investing heavily in building up its own rare earth supply chains across the world, these projects will likely take years to bear fruit.
Di Meglio said that behind the smiles and handshakes at Shenzhen was a growing effort by both countries to extract themselves from their decades-old economic interdependence.
“There is both a willingness to decouple and, at the same time, the recognition that this decoupling can’t happen overnight, that it has to be managed,” he said. “And the ones who have already have a head start on this decoupling are the Chinese, because they saw this decoupling coming and entered into what’s called an autonomous war economy – and much more so than the US. But everyone is on this same path now.”

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO live updates: AI lab tops $2 trillion market cap in debut
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO live updates: AI lab tops $2 trillion market cap in debut
articles.content_orig:
CEO of Anthropic Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei, Co-founder and President of Anthropic embrace alongside board members inside the Nasdaq MarketSite ahead of their anticipated IPO in New York City on November 19, 2026. CHARLY TRIBALLEAU/AFP via Getty Images hide caption
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
Shares in the artificial intelligence giant Anthropic soared in their market debut after the company raised more than $100 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering and private placement that valued it at around $1.5 trillion.
It's a remarkably rapid ascent for the five-year-old AI company, and a sign of strong investor appetite despite growing concern about a possible AI bubble.
Anthropic sold 956 million shares — far more than originally planned  — at an IPO price of $83 per share, it announced on Wednesday. That price exceeded its targeted range of $70 to $78 per share.
The company's seven founders also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO. On top of that, Anthropic's prospectus included plans to put an additional $26 billion worth of shares into the market through private placements with companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
The total haul is more than $107 billion.
The amount of money raised makes Anthropic's IPO the biggest in history, after Elon Musk's mega-conglomerate SpaceX landed $75 billion when it listed in June.
Anthropic's shares opened trading on the Nasdaq under the ticker symbol ANT at $111.50, a whopping 34% above the IPO price.
Anthropic's rise has been meteoric.
"We've never seen a company that's able to grow this fast [and] be this dominant," said Andrew Rocco, a stock analyst at the financial research firm Zacks.
Anthropic got its start in 2021 as a breakaway group of researchers who once worked for ChatGPT-maker OpenAI. Led by now-CEO Dario Amodei, the Anthropic founders were concerned that OpenAI, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.
Amodei and the others quickly raised hundreds of millions of dollars and set out to develop AI models in a way that the company said focused on safety and "alignment," or the idea that AI should be harmless and act in ways that jibe with human values and intent.
Anthropic launched Claude in early 2023, just months after OpenAI released ChatGPT. Ever since, the two companies have been neck-and-neck competitors in cutting-edge artificial intelligence, known as "frontier AI." The Claude family of AI models, including the Claude chatbot and Claude Code, are among the most popular and powerful in the world, and have helped transform everything from online search to software engineering.
They are also the San Francisco-based company's main source of income, according to its IPO prospectus, which said revenue in the first half of the year skyrocketed 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, versus a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.
The IPO comes at a time when shares in tech companies linked to the AI boom have been volatile. Investors have vacillated between enthusiasm for what many believe will be a revolutionary technology and concern that the vast sums of money being poured into it may be hard to justify.
"It's going to be a test of investor sentiment towards the AI trade," said Janice Quek, an equity analyst at the investment research firm CFRA. "We've seen in recent weeks that there has been a lot of pressure and really market sell-offs on the AI ecosystem just because a lot of people are worried about the AI bubble, for example, or the concerns around AI financing and whether there's a return on investment on AI."
The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down more than 11% since early October.
Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, an early Anthropic investor, told a Semafor conference on Monday the IPO is one of the best ways to invest in AI applications. He said his firm had trimmed its exposure to AI infrastructure — companies involved in things like manufacturing semiconductors and building data centers — but that Altimeter had requested an allotment of Anthropic stock worth $5 billion.
"I've been waiting for it," he said of the IPO. "We put in for the largest request in the 20-year history of our firm."
There is indirect evidence in Anthropic's prospectus that businesses, rather than individual subscribers, are its biggest source of revenue. Malik Ahmed Khan, an equity analyst at Morningstar, says the company's long-term success may hinge on those companies' pace of adoption of AI technologies, but it's unclear how fast that will be.
"Radios went from like 10% penetration to 90% penetration in the U.S. within a decade. Washing machines, to reach that level of penetration, took a multi-decade period," he said. "So when we're thinking about Anthropic and broadly AI in the enterprise setting, what does that adoption curve look like?"
Anthropic has not been without controversy. Earlier this year it became embroiled in a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used. The Pentagon wanted the military to be able to deploy Anthropic's models without restriction, but Amodei drew a line at fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans. The Pentagon subsequently labeled Anthropic a "supply chain risk," a designation previously reserved for foreign adversaries.
And skeptics have criticized Amodei's rapid push to develop AI despite his own dire warnings about the technology's risks . In September, Amodei wrote an essay urging his AI competitors to " pace the frontier ," or to slow down development of the most cutting-edge models and make sure that safety incidents are being reported and scrutinized by third-party auditors.
On Thursday, Amodei said the company's principles would not change.
"To state it unequivocally, we will pace the training and deployment of AI systems, taking as long as is necessary to have confidence that they are safe and will remain under human control," he said at the opening bell ceremony to start the Nasdaq exchange's trading day. "We will not bend to either business nor political pressure. Today puts the company in a stronger financial position, and in doing so, only strengthens our resolve to do the right thing."
That essay followed a summer when AI agents from Anthropic's lab, as well as OpenAI and other competitors, were revealed to have hacked other companies , setting off a frenzy of concern about the risks of rogue agents . This week, California sued OpenAI over its agents that hacked into Hugging Face, an open-source software platform.
Anthropic's IPO prospectus dedicated dozens of pages to potential risks, including the possibility that people could lose control of AI, or that AI could take harmful actions on its own.
The company also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash. Indeed, the IPO comes just weeks after midterm elections in the United States, which analysts say likely herald a period of elevated scrutiny and oversight for AI firms. Data centers became a hot-button issue this election cycle , and tech stocks sank after the election as investors anticipated that the incoming Congress would crack down on the industry.
Still, Anthropic's prospectus was bullish about the development and spread of AI. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said.
OpenAI had been on track to also list shares this year, but CEO Sam Altman postponed those plans, likely to next year, after the Hugging Face incident. At the Semafor conference on Monday Altman promised: "We will go public at some point."
"The world as a whole would like exposure to this," he continued. "And I think that's, you know, directionally a good thing to do."

articles.title_orig: Trump calls China trip ‘Great and Highly Consequential,’ announces Friday news conference
articles.title_zh: Trump calls China trip ‘Great and Highly Consequential,’ announces Friday news conference
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON — President Trump has announced that he will hold a lunchtime press conference at the White House Friday to discuss his trip to Asia .
“Heading back to Washington, D.C., from China. It was a Great and Highly Consequential Trip. I will be giving a News Conference tomorrow at 12 P.M., the White House,” Trump wrote on Truth Social while aboard Air Force One Thursday.
The president capped his whirlwind three-day trip with a historic meeting involving Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping. Trump and Xi also held a separate bilateral meeting to discuss trade issues.
During an earlier phone interview with NBC News, the president claimed “ fantastic relationships ” had been built during the summit, during which he and Xi discussed artificial intelligence — or super intelligence (SI), as Trump prefers to call it.
“We spoke about SI, and we both agreed that we want — we’re, you know, very much into SI, but we do think that having guardrails, you know, at least on a minimal basis is a positive thing,” Trump said, adding that the pair “didn’t get into definitions.”
Asked about Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s exclusion from the talks, Trump reassured Kyiv that he wouldn’t be making any decisions about Ukraine’s future without their input.
“I agree with him,” Trump also said of Zelensky. “I wouldn’t do anything without — he’s the head of that country, so I wouldn’t be doing that.”
Trump also visited the Philippines on the first leg of his trip and said he’d be discussing trade deals with the island nation along with pacts involving Thailand as well as other countries Friday.
This is a developing story. Please check back for updates.

articles.title_orig: Trump, Xi and Putin Seek to Project Power at Their First Summit
articles.title_zh: Trump, Xi and Putin Seek to Project Power at Their First Summit
articles.content_orig:
Russia’s President Vladimir Putin, China’s President Xi Jinping, and U.S. President Donald Trump pose for photos as they arrive for a trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Summit in Shenzhen on Nov. 19, 2026.
It was the first-ever meeting of the leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers—one that host Xi Jinping opened by hailing its “pioneering significance.”
Exactly what was achieved when Xi met with Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump at Kylin Villa in northwestern Shenzhen on Thursday, however, has onlookers scratching their heads. Xi started by invoking the responsibility of Great Powers toward world peace; Putin delved into historic “shared interests;” while Trump immediately lashed out at “rogue globalist organisations,” such as the International Criminal Court (ICC).
The ICC “has gotten out of control,” Trump told his companions seated around a round wooden table, and has “really strayed far beyond its jurisdiction.”
It was almost as if this historic trilateral , held on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit, didn’t have any fixed agenda. It hadn’t. When the confab was first proposed, Putin wanted to talk about Ukraine, though U.S. officials pushed back. Trump instead suggested nuclear arms and Iran, but Beijing wasn’t keen. Finally, China’s Foreign Ministry settled on “safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability in major-power relations.”
It was therefore an occasion rich with platitudes but not a lot else. “In this global village, major countries shoulder special responsibilities,” said Xi, who also called for the destruction of all nuclear weapons. “Positive interaction among major powers is not an optional question, but a compulsory one.”
Still, the meeting served its purpose. Trump gained a chance to project influence after chastening midterms and the unfolding Nvidia saga that forced the resignation of his close friend Jensen Huang as CEO. Xi got to flaunt himself as the consummate statesman, while Putin took a baby step out from the diplomatic cold. But it was also a distinctly unsettling sight for the U.S. President to be sitting beside two of America’s most consequential adversaries, whose governments declared in 2022 that their friendship with each other had “no limits.”
Before the three-way meeting, Trump met separately with Putin and then Xi. His roughly 40 minutes with the Russian President began on a hopeful note: “Wonderful things can come out of this—or at least start,” Trump said. During an hour of talks with Xi, Trump returned to a more familiar concern. “I’ll be asking you to do some more for our farmers,” he said. He also suggested that Washington and Beijing could work together to end Russia’s war in Ukraine.
That prospect mattered to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky, who said Wednesday that the war could end in a single meeting if the U.S. and China used their economic leverage against Moscow. Instead, Trump launched a broadside against the ICC, which has issued an arrest warrant against Putin for war crimes, urging his autocratic counterparts to cooperate on “ways to protect our nations’ sovereignty.”
Trump also said it was “vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world,” before segueing into a justification of his war in Iran : “That’s what we’re doing in Iran. We’re not going to let Iran have a nuclear weapon.”
Of course, this was always going to be an occasion that would put style over substance. On Wednesday, Xi surprised onlookers by greeting a clearly delighted Trump on the tarmac at Shenzhen Baoan Airport. Their handshake turned into a brief hug, before five People’s Liberation Army J-10C fighter jets flew overhead, billowing red, yellow, and blue smoke.
In personally meeting Trump as he deplaned Air Force One, Xi reciprocated the welcome he received from the U.S. President at Joint Base Andrews in September. The gesture was a first by a top Chinese leader since Mao Zedong met Nikita Khrushchev at Beijing’s airport in 1959.
Putin had to suffice with being greeted by Xi’s chief of staff, Cai Qi, upon his earlier arrival in the wee hours of Wednesday morning. But Xi spent much of that afternoon in talks with his embattled Russian counterpart, who used his speech to assembled CEOs to lambast Western sanctions, crowing that the U.S. and Europe had “punished themselves” with punitive measures, which Russia had successfully sidestepped anyway.
Upon emerging from his two-hour bilateral with Putin, Xi called on both countries to “lead and advance … the democratization of international relations.” Putin, in turn, boasted that economic coercion was “a thing of the past.” Later in the evening, Putin and Trump shook hands before the gala dinner as Xi looked on smiling.
“Beijing’s top priority would be to create a more stable external environment for China’s development, particularly by making relations with Washington more predictable while maintaining steady cooperation with Moscow,” says Sun Chenghao, a fellow with Tsinghua University’s Centre for International Security and Strategy.
Still, the summit threatened to be overshadowed by the Nvidia scandal, with company founder Huang admitting an affair with a woman accused of illicitly funneling chips to China and whom U.S. intelligence agencies reportedly suspect may be a Chinese spy. On Nov. 16, the U.S. Commerce Department issued an interim rule aimed at stopping Chinese firms from accessing advanced U.S. chips through data centers abroad.
Trump told Fox News that he and Xi “spoke the whole evening” during Wednesday’s gala dinner but only “briefly” discussed Nvidia. Trump also claimed he was unaware of the espionage allegations, which China vehemently denies. “I haven’t heard that she was a spy,” Trump said. “She was a businesswoman who bought chips, and who knows if they were bought right or wrong.”
Trump also appeared to shoot down any hopes of regulation governing AI: “We oppose any form of globalist regulation or anything to control or stifle [AI], and we won’t allow that to happen,” he said.
Still, the historic trilateral did succeed in visibly placing China at the center of Great Power diplomacy. Hosting the leaders alongside APEC supports Beijing’s claim that global influence is shifting eastward, with China as a stabilizing power, particularly amid unpredictable U.S. policy.
“The optics might actually play well for China,” says Chong Ja Ian, a professor of international relations at the National University of Singapore. “It certainly would fit the sort of image that Beijing and Xi would like to create for themselves.”
But while APEC was created in 1989 to ease trade and investment across the region, today’s world has been gripped by rising protectionism. The Trump Administration has levied tariffs on 60 trading partners that together account for 99.4% of U.S. imports, according to the Office of the U.S. Trade Representative. Moreover, Europe is increasingly chary about cheap Chinese exports that Brussels says are fueled by subsidies and industrial overcapacity.
Xi used his Wednesday address to business leaders to promise a more open Chinese market and present the world’s second-largest economy as a source of opportunity. “History tells us that opening doors brings progress while closing doors leaves one behind,” he said.
Yet the image of three elderly leaders debating global problems behind closed doors sits uneasily beside Xi’s call for a more multipolar world. Pro-Kremlin media was especially keen to frame the meeting as Yalta 2.0 after the historic powwow between Roosevelt, Stalin, and Churchill toward the end of World War II.

articles.title_orig: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
articles.title_zh: Trump accused of falling asleep during Xi Jinping speech at Apec summit in China
articles.content_orig:
US president appeared to doze off while Chinese leader made speech, but White House insisted he was awake
Donald Trump was, again, accused of falling asleep during a televised event, this time during the speech of the Chinese president, Xi Jinping, at the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in China.
The US president appeared to close his eyes for roughly 10 seconds on Thursday. As his eyes closed, Trump’s head tilted downward, and his hands remained clasped in front of him.
Several prominent Trump critics on social media alleged that the US president was asleep, including Republicans Against Trump , California governor Gavin Newsom’s press office and conservative lawyer George Conway .
White House officials denied the allegations, claiming the 80-year-old US president was looking down at papers in front of him.
“Fake News! President Trump was looking at papers in front of him while the speaker made remarks. You can clearly see his eyes move back and forth,” Steven Cheung, the White House director of communications, wrote on X in response to a Newsweek article.
“This is why the people despise media so much. They constantly lie,” Cheung added.
Trump often faces accusations of falling asleep during televised events such as Oval Office press conferences, cabinet meetings and sporting events.
Occasionally, while listening to other people speak, the US president will close his eyes for several seconds, appearing as though he is falling asleep . Despite footage of the instances going viral, the White House and Trump allies have insisted the US president does not fall asleep during meetings.
Administration officials have excused Trump’s apparent drowsiness as blinking or an example of the president listening intently. They consistently claim Trump “doesn’t sleep”.
Marco Rubio, the US secretary of state, testified to lawmakers earlier this year that he had “never seen” Trump fall asleep.
“On the contrary, the guy doesn’t sleep, which is a big problem because he calls me at two in the morning,” Rubio said in June.
Last year, JD Vance said that Trump hardly ever sleeps, even while traveling overnight.
“If we go on a 20-hour trip somewhere, he doesn’t sleep the entire time. And of course, if he’s not sleeping, if he’s working, he expects everybody else to be working too,” Vance told Fox News .
Trump became the oldest US president ever inaugurated when he was sworn in nearly two years ago. Despite his age, Trump often claims he is in near-perfect health , often bragging about his “perfect” cognitive test results and insisting he has a lot of energy.

articles.title_orig: AMD shares slide as report says China links could invite US scrutiny
articles.title_zh: AMD shares slide as report says China links could invite US scrutiny
articles.content_orig:
Shares of chipmaker Advanced Micro Devices were down about 7% Wednesday after investment firm Hunterbrook Media issued a report alleging that the company "has its own China problem."
Hunterbrook disclosed that it had taken a short position in AMD.
The report claims that "after the U.S. blacklisted Chinese server maker IEIT Systems, the company kept getting newer AMD firmware, which enables AMD chips to run in servers."
CNBC did not independently verify this information.
Hunterbrook also said that new export rules in Washington could "tighten restrictions on AMD's foreign business," alleging that AMD "bills over 20% of its revenue to customers in China and Hong Kong," and "depends on a Chinese partner to finish most of its chips."
The allegations come amid investigations of rival chipmaker Nvidia over its sales to companies in Asia with ties to China. AMD has been viewed as a beneficiary of the uncertainty surrounding Nvidia.
AMD did not immediately reply to a CNBC request for comment.
Lisa Su, CEO of AMD, said on the company's recent earnings call that China is an "important" market and that the semiconductor giant wants to be fully compliant with U.S. export controls.
_src_links: AMD shares slide as report says China links could invite US scrutiny

articles.title_orig: Anthropic IPO Live Updates: AI Firm Set to Begin Trading at $83 a Share Under ANT
articles.title_zh: Anthropic IPO Live Updates: AI Firm Set to Begin Trading at $83 a Share Under ANT
articles.content_orig:
WHEN: Today, Thursday, November 19
Below is the unofficial transcript of CNBC's exclusive interview with Anthropic co-founders Dario and Daniela Amodei today, Thursday, November 19, following the company's highly anticipated IPO. Following are links to video on CNBC.com: https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/anthropic-ceo-on-scaling-laws-i-dont-think-we-really-believed-it-until-it-actually-happened.html , https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/anthropics-debut-is-one-stop-on-the-journey-says-daniela-amodei.html , https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/dario-amodei-weare-hoping-to-be-investment-grade-in-the-future.html , https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/dario-amodei-on-if-jensen-huang-should-come-back-as-ceo-.html , and https://www.cnbc.com/video/2026/11/19/anthropic-sibling-founders-reflect-on-ipo-journey.html .
All references must be sourced to CNBC.
ANDREW ROSS SORKIN: Hey, thanks, Carl. Big day here. And I am here with the co-founders of this company, brother and sister. It's an unbelievable story, Dario and Daniela Amodei. Thank you for being here. Congratulations on this big moment.
DANIELA AMODEI: Thank you for having us.
DARIO AMODEI: Thank you for having us.
SORKIN: Here's where I want to start this. When I first met you, you basically just practically started the company. And I'm so curious — you understood scaling laws at the beginning, perhaps better than anybody, but did you ever expect three, four, five years later here we would be and be talking about evaluation that starts with a T?
DARIO AMODEI: You know, the funny thing is, you look at the scaling laws and they're a line on a piece of paper, right? They predict that a model will have certain cognitive capabilities that will be capable of certain economic tasks. But it's one thing to kind of draw that line, and it's a totally different thing to see the consequences out in the world. And so I would say the scaling laws kind of imply that the technology and hopefully our work within it would — would have this scale. But I don't think we really believed it until it actually happened.
SORKIN: And it's happening right now. Daniela, this is now going to be the largest public benefit corporation to go public. What — for those folks who are watching this morning, even thinking about investing in the company, what does that mean, both for the company itself, but also the way investors should think about that?
DANIELA AMODEI: So, as a public benefit corporation, you know, part of why we decided to incorporate this way, is Anthropic mission is so much about how do we build something that is good for everybody? How do we really build for the public benefit? And part of what I think is so interesting about this structure is that we're actually legally required to balance shareholder interest with the public benefit, with the public good. And I think when Dario and I and our other co-founders were starting the organization, you know, we learned about this concept of a public benefit corporation. It really spoke to us, because we said, well, that's exactly what we're trying to do. We're really trying to do something that we do think can have this incredible economic value and impact, but we want it to be baked into essentially our structure that we also have to balance that against building things that are good for people.
SORKIN: OK, so here's the question. How do you balance the idea of growth and the idea of, for example, pacing at this point? This is something you have talked a lot about, pacing, given some of the safety concerns around AI? And how should the investor class think about those competing interests?
DARIO AMODEI: So, this, you know, this is one of the central tensions at the heart of the company. But it's really, because this technology is so powerful, it has so many effects in the world, it's something that every company in this space will have to face, whether they want to or not. We're just facing it more explicitly and more thoughtfully. And so, you think about something like pacing, the idea behind pacing was, you know, imagine that you have — you're driving your car at 60 miles an hour, and then you discover or invent something that could let you drive the car at 200 miles an hour, right? This is models building themselves, recursive self-improvement. What we have done with pacing is essentially said, look, you know, we could drive at 200 miles an hour. Maybe let's only drive at 90 miles an hour, spend time figuring out how to do that safely, and the rest of that surplus, we spend building the model in the right way. And you know, I think, in the long run, that will work out pretty well for the investors as well, because the company that builds the safest, that has trust of the customers and the enterprises of the world, I think that is the company that's going to be both best for society and, in the long run, I hope, best for the performance of the company. And I think that's what we often look for. We look for synergies, ways to make the two line up in the long run.
SORKIN:  What does success look like today? When we see the price of this, do you say to yourself, if this is up 10 percent, 20 percent, that's success? If it's up too much, is that not success? What does, I mean, you guys have spent a lot of time with your bankers and—
DARIO AMODEI:  I think that's one of the very few topics we're not allowed to talk about.
DANIELA AMODEI:  I think, you know, I think maybe the way I would put it is, Anthropic has always been a very long-term-focused company, right? We have always been thinking about, how is this technology going to be beneficial to people in the future, but also what can it do for people today? And so while today is a super exciting milestone and we're obviously really, really excited about it, I think it's, for us, it's like one stop on the journey, right? We think about this as, wow, this is an incredible moment for Anthropic, for our mission, but we're going to wake up tomorrow and we're going to be the same company. And I think that's really, at least for me, what I have been focusing on today.
SORKIN:  The rate of growth of this company has been extraordinary, but I want to understand the unlock and also understand the competition in the space, because, increasingly, you have open-weight models. You have competitors in OpenAI, which are trying to offer tokens at cheaper prices. You have folks like Microsoft, which offer your services, and yet are also trying to sell their own models. And they say oftentimes that some of those models, or at least some of the features of their models, can do some of the same things, maybe not at the frontier level. How do you think about that in terms of what that means longer term to the margins for the company?
DARIO AMODEI:  So, I think, I think a couple concepts. One concept is the frontier. And we have found that there are these incredible returns to the frontier. And in most products or goods, you have competition on price. Here, the competition is really on quality, because the returns to greater cognitive ability are so high, right? As we climb the exponential of cognitive ability, you go from doing chatbots, to being able to do coding, to being able to do biology and robotics. And the economic value of things further along the frontier is so much larger than things earlier in the frontier that that's where most of the value accumulates. The second idea is that, if you're good at the frontier, you are also good at producing smaller and more efficient models away from the frontier. So, if you look at Haiku 5.5, we were able to drop the price by 4X from Haiku 4.5 and by many times from Opus and Fable 5 family, which are, which it's, which it's much cheaper than. And so we are able to also compete using our, the same technology that we build our models, models on the frontier, the same compute multipliers, to make these cheap models that compete away from the frontier.

articles.title_orig: Live Updates: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.title_zh: Live Updates: U.N. Court Rules Myanmar Committed Genocide Against Rohingya
articles.content_orig:
In a landmark verdict, the United Nations’ top court has ruled that Myanmar committed genocide against the Muslim minority Rohingya population in a brutal 2017 military crackdown that drove more than 730,000 Rohingya to flee to neighbouring Bangladesh.
The ruling at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) at The Hague on Thursday is the first time a state has been found responsible for genocide at the court, and only the fourth time since the Nazi Holocaust that an international court ruled that the crime had been committed.
ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said the court, in a 9-6 decision, found that Myanmar “has committed genocide against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine state, in violation of its obligations under the Genocide Convention”.
Evidence showed Myanmar forces killed 10,000 Rohingya people, Iwasawa said during a three-hour readout of the verdict.
“The Court finds that Myanmar’s security forces killed thousands of Rohingya civilians, perpetrated widespread acts of sexual violence, as well as acts of extreme violence against children, and attacked fleeing Rohingya as they sought to flee in large numbers to Bangladesh,” he said.
In specific cases that he referred to, Iwasawa said Myanmar had acted with “genocidal intent”.
The Special Advisory Council for Myanmar welcomed the judgement but stressed that the decision must lead to concrete accountability measures and reparations for victims.
Founding member Yanghee Lee said in a statement that it was a “deeply emotional day for all Rohingya people” adding “justice has been decided, but not yet delivered.’
“For decades, the Burmese military tried to erase our identity, deny our existence, and dismiss our suffering,” said Wai Wai Nu, executive director of the Women’s Peace Network and a former political prisoner.
“By finding that Myanmar committed genocide, ordering a guarantee of non-repetition, and ordering restitution and compensation, the world’s highest court has permanently shattered that state-sponsored lie,” she said.
Gambia, which brought the case to the court, called the ruling “a historic day for international justice” and urged Myanmar to comply “fully and without delay”.
British Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said the UK would expel Myanmar’s defence attache and called for an urgent UN Security Council session to discuss the judgement.
Myanmar claimed its crackdown was in response to attacks on police posts by fighters from the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army (ARSA).
The ICJ said that the “only reasonable inference” from evidence of widespread atrocities by Myanmar security forces is that they had the intent to destroy a “substantial part” of the Rohingya minority.
It said Myanmar should have known that there was a risk of genocide when armed civilians participated in the military campaign. “Myanmar thus violated its obligation to prevent genocide,” it added.
Myanmar is now obliged to provide reparations and restitution “as a result of Myanmar’s wrongful acts”, Iwasawa said.
The court said appropriate restitution by Myanmar would include: Facilitating the safe and voluntary return of Rohingya; returning or replacing all collective property damaged; facilitating the search for the disappeared and ensuring proper burials; providing for the physical and psychological rehabilitation of those mentally injured; and ensuring the population’s protection from persecution.
The court established that at least four genocidal acts have been proven, said Al Jazeera’s Step Vaessen, reporting from the Hague. They are the mass killing of civilians; the forced displacement of hundreds of thousands of people; serious harm inflicted upon the group; and the prevention of birth.
The Rohingya have long been treated as second-class citizens, well before 2017, according to the judge, Vaessen said. They were also forced to take part in a birth control programme, she added.
“So the judge really saw this as a very strong explanation that … a genocidal act was committed there.”
The verdict is “extremely important for the Rohingya,” our correspondent said. “They’ve been waiting for 10 years for any kind of justice, but it’s also important for the whole international community because genocide is such a difficult act to prove.”
The hardest part of any genocide case is proving specific intent to destroy a group in whole or in part – an extremely high bar – said Toby Cadman, an international human rights lawyer. He noted that the ICJ had never before ruled that a state has specific intent to commit genocide.
“The court is guided by the genocide convention and what the genocide convention states and it is a high threshold,” Cadman told Al Jazeera.
Human rights organisations welcomed the judgement. “We hope this ruling marks the beginning of a long overdue process of accountability in Myanmar,” Amnesty International said in a statement. It added that all crimes under international law “must be effectively investigated and those suspected of responsibility brought to justice”.
Cadman said that the situation does not come to an end with the ICJ’s ruling and a lot will depend on what comes next. This includes whether the issue goes before the UN Security Council and whether there are sanctions, or other remedies that the court can order to ensure it is enforced.
More than 1.3 million Rohingya remain displaced across South and Southeast Asia, including 1.2 million in sprawling refugee camps in Cox’s Bazar in Bangladesh, according to the UN. Conflict, shrinking humanitarian aid and dangerous sea crossings continue to leave many members of the community displaced and vulnerable.

articles.title_orig: How woman was drugged by husband and raped by strangers over 13 years
articles.title_zh: How woman was drugged by husband and raped by strangers over 13 years
articles.content_orig:
Four men have been found guilty of sexually abusing a woman whose husband drugged and secretly advertised her for sex on the internet, in the first trial of its kind in the UK.
Philip Young, 50, had already pleaded guilty to multiple charges of drugging and raping his wife, Joanne Young, over a 13-year period at their home in Swindon, Wiltshire.
Norman Macksoni, 48, Richard Wilkins, 62, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, and Mohammed Hassan, 38, were found guilty of multiple sexual offences by a jury at Winchester Crown Court. Wilkins and Macksoni were each found guilty of one count of rape.
Joanne Young, who divorced Philip Young last year, beamed at police as she left court wiping her eyes.
On the steps outside the court, Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity, said the abuse had "cost me my life as I knew it".
"The person I trusted most in the world betrayed me in the most horrific way.
"This has resulted in a devastating impact on the lives of myself and my children."
She continued: "What happened to me was not the act of one man alone, others were invited to take part and they chose to.
"That choice makes them complicit in what was done to me and today's verdicts recognise that."
She said the verdicts were significant "more broadly for women and girls who have been abused by men," sending the message "that you can be believed and understood".
She urged the government to look at the law of consent "as a priority" so that women were "properly protected in the future", adding her abuse case raised "serious questions".
Judge Mr Justice Saini had asked for calm as the verdicts were read out, with Joanne Young sitting in the public gallery surrounded by her family, her hands clasped over her mouth.
She gasped as the first guilty verdicts were read out against Connor Sanderson-Doyle, who dropped his head as he was convicted of one count of sexual assault by touching and one count of sexual assault by penetration.
The jury of eight men and four women also convicted Wilkins of one count of assault by penetration.
Hassan was found guilty of one count of sexual assault by touching.
A sixth defendant, Dean Hamilton, 47, of Street, in Somerset, admitted one charge of assault by penetration, two of sexual assault and one of rape at an earlier court hearing in February.
The judge commended Joanne Young and said she had shown "amazing bravery through these proceedings".
One police officer could also be seen sobbing as they left the court.
As all defendants were led from the courtroom after being told by the judge to expect lengthy jail terms when they are sentenced on 21 and 22 December, Joanne Young's family could be seen hugging.
Philip Young - who served as a Conservative Swindon borough councillor between 2007 and 2010 - drugged and raped his wife over 13 years and invited the men via websites and apps such as Craigslist, Grindr and Fab Swingers to have sex with her without her knowledge.
He pleaded guilty at an earlier court hearing to 56 charges made up of 14 counts of voyeurism, 11 of rape, 11 of administering a substance with intent, seven of assault by penetration, four of sexual assault and one of publishing obscene articles in relation to his wife.
James Foster, specialist Crown Prosecution Service (CPS) prosecutor, said: "This is the first time in the UK that a jury have convicted or been asked to consider a case of organised drug-facilitated sexual abuse, which has been organised by the husband."
The crimes of the former Tory councillor emerged after the highly publicised case in France of Gisèle Pelicot, whose husband, Dominique Pelicot, drugged and raped her and invited 50 other men to abuse her. Gisèle Pelicot also waived her right to anonymity in that trial.
Her husband was jailed for 20 years in France in 2024 and all the defendants were found guilty of at least one charge.
Police and prosecutors building the case against Philip Young sought the expertise of the French investigators to assist them in bringing him to justice.
Detectives discovered that Philip Young, whose most recent address was in Enfield, north London, had taken 480 intimate images and videos of his wife on 200 occasions and posted images online on at least 500 occasions – with the vast majority of these taken at the family home in Swindon.
The trial of the four defendants heard the investigation into Philip Young had begun after police were alerted to the fact he had uploaded extreme pornographic images to the internet in 2023.
Wiltshire Police said it was still looking for another man wanted in connection with alleged sex offences against Joanne Young.
The force released five images of a bald man taken between April and May 2022.
They described him as being of "a large build, hairy, with scarring on the back of his head, prominent lips, short or shaved hair, and a distinctive tattoo on the left side of his chest".
Wiltshire Police added the extent of drug-rape offences was unknown because victims might not know they had been targeted.
A police spokesperson said: "While cases involving organised drug-facilitated sexual assault remain relatively rare compared to other forms of sexual offending, intelligence and other recent cases would suggest this may be a significantly under-reported crime type.
"Victims are often unaware they have been drugged, may have fragmented memories of events, or may initially attribute symptoms to alcohol consumption.
"These factors make detection and reporting particularly challenging."

articles.title_orig: A third Ukrainian strike in 4 days halts rail traffic on Russia’s Kerch Bridge to Crimea
articles.title_zh: A third Ukrainian strike in 4 days halts rail traffic on Russia’s Kerch Bridge to Crimea
articles.content_orig:
Russian president makes remarks after Ukraine strikes strategic bridge to Crimea for third time in a week
Vladimir Putin has said Russia’s response to the bombing of the Kerch bridge to Crimea will be “painful”, after Ukraine attacked the strategic connection for the third time this week.
The warning was delivered at a press conference after Putin met Donald Trump and Xi Jinping in China. The Russian president claimed he had been considering agreeing to local ceasefires until the Kerch road bridge was destroyed.
“After the strikes on the Crimean Bridge, we will not negotiate,” Putin said, insisting the bridge was only used by civilians. “We will respond to these attacks. Our response will be far more painful than Kyiv’s attack on the bridge.”
A series of explosions were heard in the Ukrainian capital in the mid-afternoon, and there were reports that a Russian drone had struck near the Dutch embassy in Kyiv, though it was unclear if it was deliberately targeted.
Shortly after midnight on Tuesday, Ukraine’s military blew up the central span of the Kerch road bridge in a complex air raid that involved Ruta cruise missiles made by a Dutch company as well as several Ukrainian cruise missiles and drones.
Russia had threatened the Netherlands afterwards, the Russian embassy in the country asking “Is the Dutch government openly taking part in the conflict?” after the company, Destinus, had said it was a key element in the attack.
Tom Berendsen, the Dutch foreign minister, confirmed that “a projectile struck behind” the embassy in Kyiv. “Fortunately, our colleagues are unharmed, though there is some minor damage to the building,” he said, adding that officials were now investigating the incident.
One person, a man aged 26, was killed and five others were injured in the afternoon attacks, city authorities said.
The destruction of the Kerch bridge was deliberately timed, Ukrainian military sources said , to embarrass Putin before the extraordinary summit in which the Russian president sat down with Trump and Xi to discuss the war and other issues.
It was followed up, on Wednesday night, by a further attack on the remaining rail bridge to Crimea. Train services were halted as a result of the strikes, conducted, Ukraine’s military said, with Neptune missiles made in Ukraine.
Sergei Aksyonov, the Kremlin-appointed governor of Crimea, said on Wednesday night that there had been another attack on the bridge, then added on Thursday that trains would start crossing from “approximately 4pm”.
Emergency repair workers had made “heroic efforts” to restore the track, the governor said. Nobody was reported wounded as a result of the incident, Russia’s transport ministry added.
Ukraine’s military said the Kerch bridge was “the main land artery the Russian army uses to supply its occupation groupings in the south with fuel, ammunition and equipment” – in contrast to the comments made by Putin.
The $3.6bn (£2.7bn) bridge, built by Russia after its occupation of Crimea, has been struck three times in a week. Initial attacks on Monday showed that Tuesday’s full-scale assault would be possible.
A 227-metre section of the road spanning the Kerch strait collapsed into the Sea of Azov after a complex air raid that had been prepared and planned over several weeks.
A source in Ukraine’s armed forces said this week’s attacks were designed to embarrass Putin on the world stage. “The bridge is a symbol of Putin’s rule. Destroying it sends a message to the other two great leaders that Putin is not as strong as he pretends,” they said.
For Ukraine, the bridge across the Kerch strait is a hated symbol of Russian arrogance and colonial thinking. Ukraine has previously declared that the bridge, built eight years ago, is illegal. Kyiv had tried to blow it up twice in the past – with a truck bomb in 2022, and a sea drone the following year.
Zelesnkyy described the earlier attack this week as the culmination of a seven-stage campaign to demolish the bridge, largely involving domestically produced drones and ballistic missiles, clearing the radar and air defences of Russian-occupied Ukraine.
Flamingo FP-5 cruise missiles and Palianytsia drones struck the central section of the bridge, bringing down its supporting arch.

articles.title_orig: AMD sheds nearly $100 billion in market value as China chip concerns hit AI stocks
articles.title_zh: AMD sheds nearly $100 billion in market value as China chip concerns hit AI stocks
articles.content_orig:
Concerns about balance sheets and valuations in the artificial intelligence sector have hit the market hard since October, and investors who have shorted publicly traded tech companies in the AI trade have profited. Most investors don't think as much about "shorting" debt, but there will be a way through exchange-traded funds to profit from widening credit default swap spreads of top AI companies.
Both Tuttle Capital and Defiance ETFs have filed for funds that target the credit default swaps of companies closely linked to the AI trade, from CoreWeave and Oracle to the Magnificent Seven: Alphabet, Amazon, Meta Platforms, Microsoft Corporation, Nvidia, Tesla, and Apple.
Credit default swaps are contracts in which investors pay for protection in case the borrower can't repay its debt. Wider spreads indicate investors view the bonds as riskier. CDS is a closely watched indicator of issuer health in the debt markets, especially in the AI market this year. The ETFs are designed to gain when the CDS spreads of these companies widen, either as a group in the case of a Magnificent Seven CDS fund, or individually in the case of proposed ETFs targeting Oracle, CoreWeave and Meta. The funds would lose value when the market assesses the creditworthiness of these debt issuers as improving.
Both ETF managers filed for CoreWeave and Oracle CDS funds, specifically, among broader AI and semiconductor company CDS portfolios.
If the exchange-traded fund managers get approval from the Securities and Exchange Commission, these portfolios would be the first of their kind in an ETF market that has become more aggressive in recent years about launching higher-risk strategies revolving around more complex financial instruments than just public stocks and bonds. The ETF managers plan to employ leverage in the portfolios, which both increases risk and the potential for outsized returns on any given day, similar to the way existing single-stock leverage and inverse ETFs function.
The ETF managers say these CDS funds can serve an important role in a market on edge about AI debt.
"As AI infrastructure investment accelerates and companies take on significant capital commitments to fund that growth, we see an opportunity to give investors more targeted tools to manage credit risk and hedge potential financial stress across some of the biggest names driving the AI buildout," Sylvia Jablonski, CIO of Defiance ETFs, said in a statement to CNBC.
Neocloud companies like CoreWeave are a major focus for AI skeptics, an AI bubble watch compounded by the exit of Jensen Huang from Nvidia, who is seen as a critical player in financing the AI buildout, with Nvidia called by some the "central bank of AI ."
Apollo Global Management CEO Marc Rowan on Tuesday said that neocloud company AI projects could face an existential crisis if Nvidia funding dries up. "There was a strong incentive for Nvidia as a business matter to get these projects off the ground," Rowan said in an interview with CNBC's " Squawk on the Street ." "If that banking function, that guarantor function, gets taken away, access to capital for a large number of neoclouds is going to disappear."
In its earnings filings and conference call on Tuesday, Nvidia shifted the tone in discussing the way it finances the AI ecosystem.
Matthew Tuttle, founder and CEO of Tuttle Capital Management, said it is less likely that these ETFs will find an audience among retail investors than smaller institutional players.
"It may be a stretch for the average retail guy," he said, but he added that having managed leveraged and inverse ETFs, it is clear that many investors "get interested" when a particular asset is seeing outsized moves, as has been the case with AI company-linked CDS in 2026. "The stuff that moves a lot is the stuff that tends to generate the most interest," he said.
Both prospectuses stress that these funds are not designed to move inversely to the reference companies' stocks and can lose money while a company's shares decline. They also note these funds don't short bonds or bet directly against a company's stock, and to buy CDS protection, they pay premiums, which are a unique cost to the fund manager whether or not credit conditions worsen.
The CDS of these companies have been on the move in a major way as part of the AI trade over the past year.
CoreWeave's 9.75% bond due in 2031 is yielding close to 16%, while spreads on its five-year credit default swaps were recently between 1,100-1,200. Spreads over 1,000 are generally considered a sign of distress.
CoreWeave executives have taken their messaging about the debt public, with co-founder and chief strategy officer Brian Venturo posting on X.com on Wednesday that he had purchased $30 million in unsecured company bonds and was going to hold them until maturity in 2031. "I've never been more confident in CoreWeave," he wrote.
Oracle CDS contracts have moved up over the past year from below 80 to a current range above 300.
The CDS spreads on the biggest tech companies, including Amazon and Meta as examples, rose over 100% within the past year, as their free cash flow turned negative from spending heavily on AI. Even though the market is much less concerned about their balance sheets than that of the neoclouds, major tech company CDS spreads did hit five-year highs earlier this month.
Tuttle said that these ETFs, if approved, would be the "easiest" to use for smaller institutions and family offices that want CDS exposure and "are either too small to trade with the Goldmans of the world or lack the in-house expertise to trade CDS on their own."
"It is a different way to hedge the AI trade," Tuttle said.
ETF investing experts expressed skepticism about this approach and market reception. "I don't see much demand materializing for these types of products," said Nate Geraci, president of NovaDius Wealth Management. But he added it does make sense to target these ETFs "at retail investors who are seeing scary headlines around AI capex spending. Yet another way to speculate (gamble)," he said.
Todd Sohn, chief ETF strategist at Baird Strategas, said he foresees confusion with how these funds will work. "How many non-professionals know what CDS are?" he said.
Tuttle says it won't take billions in assets to make an ETF focused on AI CDS a minor financial success. "My criteria is I want to see a runway to $20 million, which is about our breakeven. I see it here. It doesn't mean it will happen, but I think we have a decent chance."
— CNBC's Michelle Fox contributed to this report

articles.title_orig: Dow falls 500 points as Anthropic IPO sparks AI rebound: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Dow falls 500 points as Anthropic IPO sparks AI rebound: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
The Anthropic website and mobile phone app are shown in this photo, in New York, Friday, July 5, 2024. Richard Drew/AP hide caption
Stay up to date with our Up First newsletter, sent every weekday morning.
Anthropic shares are about to make their market debut after the company raised more than $100 billion in a record-breaking initial public offering that valued it at around $1.5 trillion.
It's a remarkably rapid ascent for the five-year-old artificial intelligence powerhouse, and a sign of strong investor appetite despite growing concern about a possible AI bubble.
Anthropic sold 956 million shares — far more than originally planned  — at an IPO price of $83 per share, it announced on Wednesday. That price exceeded its targeted range of $70 to $78 per share.
The company's seven founders also sold more than 23 million shares as part of the IPO. On top of that, Anthropic's prospectus included plans to put an additional $26 billion worth of shares into the market through private placements with companies including Google, Microsoft and Nvidia.
The total haul is more than $107 billion.
Anthropic valuation could rise or fall later on Thursday, when its shares start trading publicly on the Nasdaq exchange under the ticker symbol ANT.
The amount of money raised makes Anthropic's IPO the biggest in history, after Elon Musk's mega-conglomerate SpaceX landed $75 billion when it listed in June.
Anthropic's rise has been meteoric.
"We've never seen a company that's able to grow this fast [and] be this dominant," said Andrew Rocco, a stock analyst at the financial research firm Zacks.
Anthropic got its start in 2021 as a breakaway group of researchers who once worked for ChatGPT-maker OpenAI. Led by now-CEO Dario Amodei, the Anthropic founders were concerned that OpenAI, run by Sam Altman, was not on a path to develop AI safely.
Amodei and the others quickly raised hundreds of millions of dollars and set out to develop AI models in a way that the company said focused on safety and "alignment," or the idea that AI should be harmless and act in ways that jibe with human values and intent.
Anthropic launched Claude in early 2023, just months after OpenAI released ChatGPT. Ever since, the two companies have been neck-and-neck competitors in cutting-edge artificial intelligence, known as "frontier AI." The Claude family of AI models, including the Claude chatbot and Claude Code, are among the most popular and powerful in the world, and have helped transform everything from online search to software engineering.
They are also the San Francisco-based company's main source of income, according to its IPO prospectus, which said revenue in the first half of the year skyrocketed 1,300% at $16.3 billion, while its adjusted operating income — a measure of potential profitability — hit $1.6 billion during the period, versus a loss of $1.8 billion the year before.
The IPO comes at a time when shares in tech companies linked to the AI boom have been volatile. Investors have vacillated between enthusiasm for what many believe will be a revolutionary technology and concern that the vast sums of money being poured into it may be hard to justify.
"It's going to be a test of investor sentiment towards the AI trade," said Janice Quek, an equity analyst at the investment research firm CFRA. "We've seen in recent weeks that there has been a lot of pressure and really market sell-offs on the AI ecosystem just because a lot of people are worried about the AI bubble, for example, or the concerns around AI financing and whether there's a return on investment on AI."
The tech-heavy Nasdaq is down more than 11% since early October.
Altimeter Capital CEO Brad Gerstner, an early Anthropic investor, told a Semafor conference on Monday the IPO is one of the best ways to invest in AI applications. He said his firm had trimmed its exposure to AI infrastructure — companies involved in things like manufacturing semiconductors and building data centers — but that Altimeter had requested an allotment of Anthropic stock worth $5 billion.
"I've been waiting for it," he said of the IPO. "We put in for the largest request in the 20-year history of our firm."
There is indirect evidence in Anthropic's prospectus that businesses, rather than individual subscribers, are its biggest source of revenue. Malik Ahmed Khan, an equity analyst at Morningstar, says the company's long-term success may hinge on those companies' pace of adoption of AI technologies, but it's unclear how fast that will be.
"Radios went from like 10% penetration to 90% penetration in the U.S. within a decade. Washing machines, to reach that level of penetration, took a multi-decade period," he said. "So when we're thinking about Anthropic and broadly AI in the enterprise setting, what does that adoption curve look like?"
Anthropic has not been without controversy. Earlier this year it became embroiled in a conflict with the Pentagon over how its models can be used. The Pentagon wanted the military to be able to deploy Anthropic's models without restriction, but Amodei drew a line at fully autonomous weapons and mass surveillance of Americans. The Pentagon subsequently labeled Anthropic a "supply chain risk," a designation previously reserved for foreign adversaries.
And skeptics have criticized Amodei's rapid push to develop AI despite his own dire warnings about the technology's risks . In September, Amodei wrote an essay urging his AI competitors to " pace the frontier ," or to slow down development of the most cutting-edge models and make sure that safety incidents are being reported and scrutinized by third-party auditors.
That essay followed a summer when AI agents from Anthropic's lab, as well as OpenAI and other competitors, were revealed to have hacked other companies , setting off a frenzy of concern about the risks of rogue agents . This week, California sued OpenAI over its agents that hacked into Hugging Face, an open-source software platform.
Anthropic's IPO prospectus dedicated dozens of pages to potential risks, including the possibility that people could lose control of AI, or that AI could take harmful actions on its own.
The company also flagged the risk of heightened scrutiny or political backlash. Indeed, the IPO comes just weeks after midterm elections in the United States, which analysts say likely herald a period of elevated scrutiny and oversight for AI firms. Data centers became a hot-button issue this election cycle , and tech stocks sank after the election as investors anticipated that the incoming Congress would crack down on the industry.
Still, Anthropic's prospectus was bullish about the development and spread of AI. "We believe this abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet," it said.
OpenAI had been on track to also list shares this year, but CEO Sam Altman postponed those plans, likely to next year, after the Hugging Face incident. At the Semafor conference on Monday Altman promised: "We will go public at some point."
"The world as a whole would like exposure to this," he continued. "And I think that's, you know, directionally a good thing to do."
Meanwhile, shares in SpaceX, the first of this year's AI mega-IPOs, are trading near their initial price of $135. After the company's June listing, the stock leapt to more than $200, then slid to as low as about $108 before recovering ground.

articles.title_orig: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
articles.title_zh: China, Russia and US agree peace declaration with no mention of Ukraine and Iran wars
articles.content_orig:
Xi, Putin and Trump outline priorities that include UN reform, boosting oil supplies and ‘protection of diplomatic immunity’
China, Russia and the US say they have agreed a peace statement after an unprecedented trilateral summit, but the declaration made no mention of the wars in Ukraine and Iran caused by two of the participants.
The declaration on Thursday also outlined a set of priorities that included changing the UN, boosting oil supplies and what it said was the protection of diplomatic immunity.
The statement affirmed that “a nuclear war cannot be won and must not be fought”, but stopped short of suggesting the beginnings of a framework for denuclearisation.
The meeting between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump has dominated the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit this week, with China, the host, promising it would be “groundbreaking”.
“We are really making history,” Trump told Xi and Putin at the start of the meeting. “No peace was ever forged by declining opportunities for engagement.”
Putin told a press conference later that the three men had had a “free discussion” and now had a “mutual understanding”.
Some had hopes that the talks, which lasted about one hour and 20 minutes, could be used to discuss reductions in arms between the world’s three largest nuclear powers. Beijing has previously rebuffed Trump’s advances to join such talks, pointing to the larger US and Russian stockpiles. On Thursday, though, Xi called for nuclear weapons to “be completely prohibited and thoroughly destroyed over time to make the world free of [them]”.
The language of the declaration around nuclear war is the same as that previously issued by the five permanent members of the UN security council, which includes France and the UK.
“The real test will be whether the three countries follow through on their stated commitment to discuss nuclear risk reduction and preventing nuclear proliferation,” said Patricia Kim, an expert on Chinese foreign policy at the Brookings Institution, a US thinktank. Even the suggestion that China would engage was significant, said Yun Sun, a senior fellow at the Stimson Center.
Analysts had said that the meeting’s primary significance was in its optics. “Overall, very little of substance seems to have been accomplished … This summit appears to have been all about the symbolism and prestige value,” said Prof William Hurst, from the University of Cambridge’s Centre for Geopolitics. Putin pushed back at the suggestion the summit had just been a photo-op. “It is a serious collaborative work,” he said.
In the declaration, the men “committed themselves to maintaining strategic stability and international security”.
First among their concerns was “promoting UN reform so that it may respond more effectively to global challenges”. Sun said this was a favourite topic of China’s and showed that Beijing was “flexing its diplomatic muscles”. She said: “It is able to set the agenda and the deliverables according to its priorities … and make other great powers accept them.”
The declaration also agreed that “the international criminal court [ICC] and other similar institutions must not abuse their jurisdiction”. Putin is subject to an ICC arrest warrant and so the clause added to the perception that he has done well from the summit. Since the 2022 invasion of Ukraine, the Russian president has been treated as an international pariah by Kyiv’s allies and he has not been to an Apec summit in years.
Hurst said: “This was no Yalta moment, but it was certainly a solid public demonstration of Russia’s (and Putin’s) continuing relevance and power. It’s yet another example of Putin playing a poor hand to maximum effect.”
Xi, his status as a global powerbroker now assured, began the morning by addressing Apec leaders, reiterating the themes of trade openness and innovation he has emphasised throughout the summit. He made an appeal for regional harmony, saying: “Members of Apec are like passengers riding the same ship. To navigate the waves of the Pacific, we must unite as one and look out for each other.”
However, Apec affairs appeared to take a back seat for most of the day, with business dominating the discussions. For all the camaraderie on display, relations are complex. Russia is under US sanctions over the Ukraine war, while China and the US spent much of the last year engaged in an escalating tit-for-tat trade war before Trump and Xi called a truce .
Trump and Putin earlier held a separate meeting – their first since August 2025 – with the US president calling the Russian his “friend”. The peace declaration said the three countries planned “to increase the production and supply of refined petroleum products for the benefit of all nations”. That was important, said Shan Guo from Hutong Research, a Shanghai-based advisory firm, but “now let’s see if the US will lift sanctions”.
Trump and Xi then held their third bilateral of this year. Xi said the US-China relationship was “generally stable and positive”, according to state media. But he cautioned Washington over Taiwan, saying the US “must keep doing the right thing to avoid major setbacks in US-China relations”.
Another watched-for topic lacking detailed findings was that of AI. Xi said the two countries should “enhance communication and coordination to guard against security risks … and ensure that AI remains under human control at all times”.
Ultimately, the lack of breakthroughs might suit China, which has no appetite to move beyond the role of convener, said Kim. “Beijing has little interest in taking on the diplomatic risks of brokering an actual peace agreement in Ukraine or resolving the conflict with Iran. That would entangle China in conflicts it would rather avoid,” she said.

"There is no disruption to our services," according to the statement.
JPMorganChase said Thursday morning that "third parties who provide services" to the banking giant "were the target of a cyberattack."
"Based on our investigation so far, we believe the attackers accessed certain marketing data held by those vendors, which may include some customer names and email addresses," the statement continued.
"There is no disruption to our services," according to the statement.
JPMorganChase, the largest U.S. bank, did not disclose when the cyberattack occurred or name the third-party companies that were targeted.
"Where appropriate, we will contact affected customers directly and offer support, including complimentary credit monitoring," the company said in its statement.
The company added that it found "no connection to service disruptions some customers experienced earlier this week."
JPMorganChase said on Monday that it experienced technical issues that triggered online delays across several major U.S. banks. Chase blamed the outage on a "software bug."
There have been several recent tech outages across the nation that affected air travel, email and hotel reservations, and even slowed classified internal communications at the National Security Agency.
Top Trump administration officials continued this week to insist that there is no evidence that those outages were the result of cyberattacks.

articles.title_orig: ‘GTA VI’ Beats ‘The Odyssey’ Revenue On Release Day, Estimate Says
articles.title_zh: ‘GTA VI’ Beats ‘The Odyssey’ Revenue On Release Day, Estimate Says
articles.content_orig:
Following 13 years of anticipation, two delayed launches, and a lot of speculation, it's finally here: Grand Theft Auto 6 officially launched at midnight, and the hype has turned into history.
Gamers in Pittsburgh and across the country made their first steps in Vice City.
"Working, playing GTA, and studying for the MCAT," said one gamer we spoke with.
That's pretty much been the new routine for millions who have been waiting since childhood to play the latest installment in the ever-popular Rockstar Games franchise.
Even if you aren't partaking in GTA 6, chances are you've heard about it. The preorders have reportedly reached nearly 16 million copies, for an estimated $1.5 billion in sales - all before the game even launched.
"I was in the bathroom the other day, and this guy was calling his friend asking if he had a PS5 or something, and was like, 'Let's hop on at midnight,'" said Gary Winthorp.
That kind of hype isn't just showing up in conversations, but in numbers, as well.
We spoke with Comcast, which said the first 48 hours of pre-downloads marked the largest standalone event in network history, even surpassing Super Bowl numbers.
"PlayStation and Xbox, there's enough data coming down through our network for a million households to stream The Odyssey epic movie in 4K for like two straight days," said Joel Shadle, VP of technology and communications with Comcast.
That's a lot of data for just one game, and with only one network, the numbers across all internet service providers are astronomical.
If you're a Comcast Xfinity customer, you actually have a perk that will help you download the 212 GB game: through December 3, customers can get a temporary boost by activating it in the app.
"Over the course of that 15 days, you'll have 2GB speeds, more than enough to download GTA," said Shadle.
Shadle added that if conditions are perfect, it will take about 30 minutes total for a download. With a slower connection, it could take hours or even days.
